title: AI Literacy & Implementation
subtitle: Understand AI, prompt it well, judge its outputs, use it ethically.
description: A 4-week journey from 'what is AI?' to 'I can use AI responsibly to do real work'. Each week pairs lessons with a hands-on practice activity — including a live AI prompt lab where you actually talk to a real model.
tagline: From 'AI is magic' to 'I can drive the AI'.

outline.outcome: Distinguish rule-based code, ML, and generative AI; spot AI in everyday life.

outline.theme: How to talk to an AI
outline.outcome: Write specific, role-set, constraint-bounded prompts; iterate; recognise hallucinations.
Identify training-data bias; articulate harms; pick ethical use cases.
Plan and execute a small real-world AI project with safety guardrails.

weeks.title: What is AI, really?
weeks.summary: Cut through the hype. By the end of this week you can tell apart rule-based programs, machine learning, and generative AI — and you can spot AI in your daily life.
weeks.homework_summary: Spot 5 AI features in apps you actually use this week.

lessons.title: Why this module exists

content.intro: AI is in your phone, your homework help, your friend's Snap filter, the YouTube recommendations on your TV. You'll spend the rest of your life with AI as a coworker. This module teaches you to be in charge of it instead of the other way around.

blocks.text: Three claims that drive this whole module: (1) AI is a tool, not a brain. (2) The skill of using AI well is closer to writing a good question than typing a search. (3) AI gets things wrong, confidently. You will learn to catch it.

blocks.title: What you'll be able to do by Week 4
blocks.text: Write effective prompts. Spot AI mistakes. Identify bias in AI outputs. Plan and run a small AI-assisted project ethically.

lessons.coaching_moment: Your goal is not to memorise AI history. It is to become a confident, sceptical user.

lessons.title: The three kinds of 'AI'

content.intro: Most people lump everything under 'AI'. There are three very different things going on:

blocks.text: 1. RULE-BASED systems. A human writes if-this-then-that. Your spam filter from 2005. Predictable. Boring. Not really 'intelligent'.
2. MACHINE LEARNING. The system learns patterns from examples. Show it 10,000 photos labelled cat/dog, it learns to label new ones. It cannot do anything it wasn't trained on.

3. GENERATIVE AI. Trained on huge amounts of text/images, it produces new content — essays, pictures, code. ChatGPT, Claude, image generators. It feels magical because it produces fluent answers — even when those answers are wrong.

blocks.title: The trap
blocks.text: Generative AI is fluent, not truthful. Fluency is NOT a sign of correctness. This is the most important sentence in this module.

lessons.coaching_moment: If a friend confidently describes the plot of a movie they never watched, that's generative AI when it hallucinates.

lessons.title: How a language model actually works (no math)

content.intro: A large language model is — at its core — a very fancy 'guess the next word' machine.

blocks.text: It read most of the public internet. It learned: given the words so far, which word probably comes next? When you give it a prompt, it just keeps picking probable next words until it reaches a stopping point.

This explains everything weird about it: why it's fluent (it's seen millions of fluent sentences), why it sometimes makes things up (the 'probable' word isn't always 'true'), and why prompts matter (changing the early words changes every probability that follows).

blocks.title: Mental model
blocks.text: Imagine the AI as a student who has read every textbook but has never been outside. They sound right. They confuse books with reality.

lessons.coaching_moment: Once you internalise 'guess the next word', AI stops being magic.

lessons.title: AI is already in your daily life

content.intro: You probably interact with AI a dozen times a day without noticing.

blocks.text: YouTube recommendations (ML pattern matching), Google Maps ETA (ML on traffic), Snap filters (computer vision), voice assistants (speech recognition + LLM), camera autofocus, spam filters, fraud detection on UPI payments, even auto-correct.
Knowing where AI is operating helps you ask 'should I trust this?' and 'is this AI working FOR me or for someone else?'

fields.question: Which is generative AI?

options.label: A spam filter that blocks emails containing 'free money'.
ChatGPT writing a four-stanza poem when you ask.

fields.explanation: Generative AI produces new content (text, images, code). The others are rule-based or pattern-matching ML.

fields.question: An AI confidently tells you 'The capital of Australia is Sydney.' This is called:
fields.explanation: When an AI confidently states something untrue, that's called a hallucination. (Australia's capital is Canberra.)

fields.question: A language model is, at its core:

options.label: A digital brain that thinks like a human.
A statistical engine that predicts the most probable next word.
A program that has memorised the entire internet.

fields.explanation: An LLM predicts probable next tokens (words/word-pieces). It doesn't 'think' or 'search' — it generates.

fields.question: Which is most likely RULE-BASED, not learning AI?

options.label: Image search returning photos of cats when you type 'cat'
An office form that won't submit unless your phone number has 10 digits
YouTube's autoplay choosing what plays next

fields.explanation: A 10-digit check is a hand-coded rule. The others rely on learned patterns.

fields.question: Why does HOW you phrase a prompt matter so much for an LLM?

options.label: It doesn't — the AI understands intent.
Because the early words shape every probability that follows.
Because the AI gets bored with short prompts.

fields.explanation: Each generated word is conditioned on everything before it — so the prompt steers the entire output.

weeks.week_recap: You can now distinguish rule-based, ML, and generative AI; you understand 'fluent ≠ truthful'; and you've audited 5 apps for AI use.

weeks.title: How to talk to an AI
weeks.summary: Prompting is a skill. This week you learn it the way professionals do — by practising on a real AI in our Prompt Lab and getting graded by an AI coach.
weeks.homework_summary: Complete all 5 tasks in the Prompt Lab with a passing score.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a great prompt

content.intro: A useful prompt almost always has five parts. Most people skip three of them.

blocks.text: ROLE — who should the AI be? (e.g., 'Act as a strict Class 8 maths tutor.')
TASK — what specific thing should it do? (e.g., 'Explain why dividing by zero is undefined.')
CONTEXT — what does it need to know? (e.g., 'I'm a 13-year-old just learning algebra.')
FORMAT — how should the output look? (e.g., '4 sentences, with one real-world analogy.')
CONSTRAINTS — what's off-limits? (e.g., 'Do not use the words infinity or undefined without explaining them.')

blocks.title: Mnemonic
blocks.text: RTCFC — Role, Task, Context, Format, Constraints. Try writing every prompt with all five for the next week.

lessons.coaching_moment: The difference between a useless AI answer and a great one is almost always in the prompt, not the model.

content.intro: First-draft outputs are often almost-right. Beginners hit retry. Pros refine in conversation.

blocks.text: If the answer is too long, ask for it shorter. If it's too formal, ask for casual. If a fact looks wrong, ask the AI to verify or cite. Each turn keeps the context, so you steer instead of restart.

blocks.title: Three magic refinement phrases
blocks.text: 'Now do it in 50 words.' — 'Use a real-world example.' — 'Pretend I'm 9 years old.'

content.intro: Generative AI will confidently give you fake citations, wrong dates, invented quotes. Fluency is not truth.

blocks.text: Three habits that catch most hallucinations: (1) Ask 'how do you know?' — it forces the AI to expose its reasoning. (2) Cross-check facts that matter against a primary source. (3) Be most suspicious when the answer sounds smoothest — that's exactly when fluency hides invention.

blocks.title: Rule
blocks.text: If a wrong answer would matter (homework graded for facts, news article you'll share), VERIFY it. Always. Every time.

lessons.title: Demo: a vague prompt vs a great one

content.intro: Look at the same task, two different prompts.

blocks.text: BAD prompt: 'help me revise biology'. The AI doesn't know your grade, scope, time, or level. You'll get a generic essay.

GOOD prompt: 'Act as a Class 8 biology tutor. I have 30 minutes to revise the chapter on cells. Build me a study plan with: 5-min recap, 15-min weak-spot drill on cell organelles, 10-min self-test (5 multiple-choice). Output as a numbered list with timings.'

blocks.title: Read those again
blocks.text: Notice: ROLE (tutor), TASK (study plan), CONTEXT (Class 8 biology, cells chapter), FORMAT (numbered list with timings), CONSTRAINTS (30 min total, must include self-test). RTCFC — all five.

lessons.title: 🚀 Play: AI Prompt Lab
lessons.context: 5 hands-on prompt-engineering challenges. You write a prompt, a real AI runs it, and an AI coach grades you against a rubric. You can iterate up to 5 times per task.
lessons.coaching_moment: When a task looks hard, write down RTCFC on paper before you type. Most students who fail a task skipped Constraints.

lessons.title: Field Mission: Use AI for one real task this week
lessons.summary: Pick a real task — a homework, a card you're writing, a recipe you want to try — and use an AI to help WITHOUT letting it do the whole thing. Save your prompts and the outputs.

content.intro: You can't learn this from a screen alone. Use AI for one real-life thing this week. The discipline: AI helps, you decide.

blocks.text: Examples: ask AI for 5 study-plan options for your weakest subject — pick one yourself. Ask AI to brainstorm 10 birthday-card lines for your grandmother — pick the one that sounds most like you. Ask AI for the 3 likeliest reasons your hand-drawn circuit isn't working — test them yourself.

fields.label: What was the real task?
Paste the prompt(s) you used.
What did the AI give you? (Summarise — don't paste all of it.)
What did YOU change, add, or reject from the AI's output?
What did you learn about prompting from this real task?

fields.question: Which of these is the WEAKEST prompt for a homework helper?

options.label: Act as a Class 8 maths tutor; explain LCM and HCF in a 5-line summary with one example.
Give me 3 practice problems on linear equations at Class 8 level, with worked solutions.
Explain factorisation in 3 sentences using a kitchen analogy.

fields.explanation: 'Help me with maths' has no role, no scope, no constraints — the AI cannot help you well.

fields.question: An AI gives you a confident-sounding fact for your project. The smartest next move is:

options.label: Use it — the AI sounds sure.
Verify the fact against a primary source before relying on it.
Ask the AI 'are you sure?' and trust the second answer.

fields.explanation: Always verify facts that matter — fluency is not truth, and asking the AI again often just produces a different confident answer.

fields.question: RTCFC stands for:

options.label: Nothing, the teacher made it up

fields.explanation: RTCFC is the five-part recipe for a great prompt.

fields.question: Your AI's first answer is too long. Best move?
fields.explanation: Iterate. The AI keeps the context — refine instead of restarting.

fields.question: When SHOULD you most distrust an AI's answer?

options.label: When it sounds smooth and confident.
When it admits it doesn't know.
When it asks you a clarifying question.

fields.explanation: Smooth fluency is exactly when hallucinations hide. Doubt, questions, and apologies are signs of better calibration.

weeks.week_recap: You can write structured prompts, iterate to refine, and spot hallucinations — and you've done it with a real AI.

weeks.title: Bias, ethics, and consequences
weeks.summary: AI is trained on humans — including human bias. This week you learn where bias comes from, how to spot it, and how to use AI ethically when it really matters.
weeks.homework_summary: Complete the ethics tribunal scenario and the bias hunting worksheet.

lessons.title: Where AI bias actually comes from

content.intro: AI bias isn't a glitch the engineers forgot to fix. It's a faithful reflection of biased data.

blocks.text: An LLM trained mostly on English internet text will: speak best in English, know more about American/European topics, default to dominant viewpoints, under-represent the Global South, and replicate stereotypes embedded in the source data.
An image generator trained on stock photos will produce 'doctor' as a man and 'nurse' as a woman — because that's the statistical pattern in the training data.

blocks.title: The honest sentence
blocks.text: AI is biased because the world is biased and AI learned from the world.

content.intro: Don't let 'bias' stay abstract. Three real ways biased AI hurts people:

blocks.text: 1. DISCRIMINATION. An AI hiring screener trained on past resumes prefers profiles like the company's existing workforce — so women and minorities get filtered out, even though no human wrote that rule.
2. MISINFORMATION AT SCALE. An LLM repeats a wrong 'fact' to a million students, and now the wrong fact is in a million essays. The internet gets dumber.
3. PRIVACY EROSION. Models trained on scraped personal data can sometimes regurgitate it — names, addresses, private text. People who never agreed to be in a dataset find themselves in one.

lessons.title: Good uses, bad uses, grey areas

content.intro: Most AI ethics is not 'should we build it' — it's 'should I, right now, in this situation, use it like this?'

blocks.text: GREEN: Brainstorming, summarising your own notes, suggesting practice questions, translating, debugging your own code, getting a second opinion on a draft you wrote.
YELLOW: Using AI to draft something you'll heavily edit and put your name on — okay if you actually edit and you're transparent. Not okay if you pretend it's all you.
RED: Submitting AI-generated work as your own original creation. Using AI to harass, deceive, or impersonate. Using AI to make decisions about people without telling them.

lessons.title: Play: Ethics Tribunal
lessons.context: Cases of AI use that went wrong. You sit on the tribunal and decide: harmful, acceptable, or grey area? Each verdict reveals consequences.
lessons.coaching_moment: There rarely is a clean 'right' answer — the skill is naming the trade-off, not pretending one doesn't exist.

lessons.title: Reflection: Where do YOU draw the line?

fields.label: Three uses of AI you think are ALWAYS okay for a Class 8 student.
Three uses of AI you think are NEVER okay for a Class 8 student.
One use that DEPENDS on the situation — and what it depends on.

fields.question: AI bias mostly comes from:

options.label: The training data reflecting the biased world

fields.explanation: Models learn statistics from the data we feed them — biased data, biased model.

fields.question: Which is GREEN-zone (clearly fine) AI use?

options.label: Submitting AI-written essay as your own work
Using AI to brainstorm 10 ideas, then picking and writing yours
Using AI to mimic your friend's voice for a prank
Asking AI to write a fake medical diagnosis

fields.explanation: Using AI to brainstorm and then doing your own work is exactly the helpful, honest pattern.

fields.question: An AI hiring tool keeps recommending male candidates. Most likely explanation:

options.label: It learned from past hiring data that was already biased

fields.explanation: Pattern matching on biased history reproduces and amplifies that bias.

fields.question: Best way to counter default AI bias when asking for examples:

options.label: Explicitly demand diversity (region, gender, era) in the prompt

fields.explanation: Force diversity in the prompt — defaults reproduce dominant patterns unless you steer.

fields.question: You used AI to draft a school speech. The honest thing to do is:

options.label: Tell people if asked, and edit it heavily so it sounds like you
Submit as-is and give the AI credit

fields.explanation: Transparency + meaningful editing is the responsible middle path.

weeks.week_recap: You can identify bias in AI outputs, articulate three concrete harms, and place real use cases on a green-yellow-red ethical map.

weeks.title: Implementing AI responsibly
weeks.summary: Time to build something. This week you plan, build, and present a small AI-assisted project — with safety guardrails — and earn your AI Literacy certificate.
weeks.homework_summary: Complete and present your AI implementation project.

content.intro: Pick something small and real — not a sci-fi vision. Three formats that work:

blocks.text: 1. AI HELPER for a real task in your life. e.g., 'Daily homework planner' — you give it your subjects + tests this week, it gives you a study schedule. You build it as a SET OF PROMPTS in a doc + a usage guide.
2. AI EXPLAINER for a topic in your school. e.g., 'Class 6 photosynthesis tutor' — a system prompt and 5 example interactions to share with younger students.
3. COMMUNITY MICRO-TOOL. e.g., 'Festival recipe assistant for elderly family who can't type long' — a prompt template + spoken-style instructions.

content.intro: Before you ship anything that uses AI, run through these five.

blocks.text: 1. WHO IS HARMED IF THE AI IS WRONG? If 'no one' — proceed. If 'someone' — add verification steps.
2. WHAT DATA AM I PUTTING IN? Don't paste private addresses, photos, medical info, or other people's content into AI.
3. AM I BEING TRANSPARENT? Anyone using your tool should know AI is in the loop.
4. WHAT'S THE FALLBACK? If the AI is offline or wrong, what does the user do?
5. WHO REVIEWS THE OUTPUT? You shouldn't ship anything with zero human-in-the-loop check, especially for a younger audience.

content.intro: Plan in hand, go build the thing. Use any AI you have access to. The deliverable is: (a) the working prompt(s) or tool, (b) a short demo with one real user, (c) a reflection on what changed during the build.

blocks.text: Pro move: keep your first version simple and test with one real user before adding features.
